issues.legal_issue: Sale transactions that are materially unlike the acquired land or involve an unusually small plot do not establish the acquired land’s comparable market value.
material_facts: The acquired land was generally described as parti land and had lain waste and unused for many years.
About two kathas of the acquired land were occupied by a ditch where deep rainwater accumulated during the monsoon.
Adjacent land had been used for dumping garbage and, for some time, as a trenching ground.
The acquired land was not fit for building and was some distance from the locality where building activity was shown.
One sale relied on involved eight kathas of land, while the other involved only one katha.
issues.conclusion: The two sale deeds were not comparable instances establishing the acquired land’s market value, and the challenge to the valuation based on those deeds failed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed by reference to relevant evidence of value; sale transactions must be comparable to the acquired land, and a sale of a very small plot may not reflect the true market value of land in the locality. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this issue.

predicates.land_acquisition_market_value_appeal: The proceeding challenges the determination of market value for land acquired through a compulsory acquisition.
predicates.acquired_site_was_materially_dissimilar_: The acquired land was waste, included a waterlogged ditch, was near land used for dumping or trenching, was unfit for building, and was away from the area of building activity, unlike the land in the relied-on sale.
predicates.second_sale_was_for_a_very_small_plot: One of the relied-on sales concerned only a small plot that could not reflect the true market value of land in the locality.

issues.definition: When a market-value appeal relies on a sale unlike the acquired site and another sale of a very small plot, those sales do not establish comparable market value.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not award compensation for an item above the Collector’s award when the claimant, after receiving notice to claim compensation, did not specify an amount for that item and had no sufficient reason for the omission.
material_facts: After receiving notice under Section 9, the claimant stated that a deep and wide well was on the land but did not claim any specific amount for it.
The Collector awarded compensation for the well, and the District Judge increased that amount.
The District Judge did not find that a sufficient reason had prevented the claimant from making a specific claim for the well.
issues.conclusion: The award for the well could not exceed the amount awarded by the Collector, and the High Court correctly reduced the District Judge’s award to that amount.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, provides that where an applicant refuses or, without sufficient reason, omits to claim compensation, the court’s award cannot exceed the amount awarded by the Collector. Section 25(1) separately limits the court’s award to the amount claimed when a claim is made pursuant to notice under Section 9. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this issue.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding concerns a court’s award of compensation for property acquired through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.claimant_received_notice_to_claim: The claimant received notice inviting a claim for compensation.
predicates.claimant_did_not_specify_compensation_fo: The claimant mentioned that a well was on the land but did not state an amount claimed for it.
predicates.no_sufficient_reason_for_omission_was_fo: The court made no finding that a sufficient reason prevented the claimant from specifying compensation for the well.

issues.definition: When a compensation appeal involves a claimant who received notice, specified no amount for the well, and had no sufficient reason for the omission, the well compensation cannot exceed the Collector’s award.
